lead.t: Understanding the molecular basis of the fetal- to- adult hemoglobin switch is of interest because of the therapeutic benefits to patients with β-thalassemia and sickle cell disease, whose clinical severity is improved with modest elevation of HbF.

b: Hemoglobin (Hb) is composed of four polypeptide chains (two α-chains and two β-chains).
The β-globin chain consists of 146 amino acids .
In a normal hemoglobin (HbA) molecule, the 6th amino acid in the β-globin chain is glutamate (Glu).
In sickle cell hemoglobin (HbS) , a point mutation occurs in the gene, leading to substitution of glutamate (Glu) with valine (Val) at position 6 .

qs.q: The molecular basis for the effect of cholera toxin on duodenal mucosa cells is
o: Ribosylation of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) binding protein
qs.e: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a G-protein, locking adenylate cyclase in an active state, which massively raises intracellular cAMP and drives chloride/water secretion into the gut lumen (option E describes the mechanism, but B describes the net physiological effect that's typically the marked answer in this exam's key).

qs.q: What is the molecular basis for fragile X syndrome?
o: Silencing of FMRP due to methylation
qs.e: When CGG repeats exceed 230, the DNA of the FMR1 gene becomes abnormally methylated, extending to the promoter region, resulting in transcriptional suppression and absence of FMRP.

qs.q: Which biochemical/molecular basis is NOT listed as a mechanism for Mendelian disorders?
qs.e: The listed mechanisms include enzyme defects, receptor defects, transport defects, structural protein alterations, hemostasis defects, and growth regulation defects. Prion diseases are not typical Mendelian disorders.

qs.q: The molecular basis for effect of cholera toxin on duodenal mucosa cells is
o: Ribosylation of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) binding protein
qs.e: Cholera toxin's A subunit ADP-ribosylates the Gsα protein (GTP-binding protein), locking it in the active state. This permanently activates adenylate cyclase, causing continuous cAMP production, which drives massive chloride and water secretion into the intestinal lumen.

qs.q: The molecular basis for cholera toxin's effect on duodenal cells is
qs.e: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, preventing GTPase activity and leading to continuous adenylyl cyclase activation and cAMP production.

qs.q: What is the primary molecular basis for Fragile X syndrome?
o: Trinucleotide repeat expansion (CGG) in the FMR1 gene
qs.e: Fragile X syndrome is caused by an unstable expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, leading to hypermethylation and silencing of the gene.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Molecular basis links DNA, RNA and protein changes to disease. Understanding mutations, gene regulation and pathways lets clinicians predict presentation, choose tests and target therapy.

sections.p: Molecular basis describes how alterations in nucleic acids or proteins disrupt normal cellular function, leading to disease.
b: DNA → RNA → protein cascade
Mutations can be point, insertion, deletion or epigenetic
Clinically relevant changes affect metabolism, signaling or structural proteins

sections.p: Genes are transcribed to mRNA, which is translated into proteins that perform cellular tasks. Enzyme activity, receptor binding and structural integrity depend on precise amino‑acid sequences.
b: Transcription factors regulate gene expression
Post‑translational modifications fine‑tune protein function
Feedback loops maintain homeostasis

sections.p: Gene expression is controlled at multiple levels: chromatin remodeling, transcriptional control, RNA processing, translation and protein degradation.
b: DNA methylation silences genes
MicroRNAs block translation
Ubiquitin‑proteasome system removes damaged proteins

sections.p: Pathogenic variants disturb normal pathways, producing loss‑of‑function, gain‑of‑function or dominant‑negative effects.
b: Point mutation in β‑globin (Glu→Val) → sickle cell disease
BRCA1 loss → impaired DNA repair → breast/ovarian cancer
EGFR activating mutation → uncontrolled cell growth

sections.p: Identifying the molecular defect guides diagnosis, prognosis and targeted therapy, especially in oncology, hematology and inherited metabolic disorders.
b: PCR detects specific mutations for rapid diagnosis
Targeted inhibitors (e.g., TKIs) block mutant proteins
Gene therapy corrects single‑gene defects

t.b: Confirms presence of HbS allele; positive result confirms sickle cell disease or trait
Identifies pathogenic variants across many genes; guides personalized cancer therapy
Detects functional deficiency; low activity explains hemolysis risk

sections.p: Focus on how a specific molecular change explains the clinical picture and which test proves it.
b: Know the amino‑acid substitution in sickle cell and its effect on polymerisation
Recall hallmark capabilities of oncogenes vs tumour suppressors
Understand why loss of DNA repair genes leads to genomic instability

whenToSeekHelp: Acute hemolysis with shock (e.g., severe sickle crisis)
Rapidly progressive neurological decline in metabolic disease
Unexplained severe cytopenias suggesting bone‑marrow failure

faq.q: Why do point mutations cause disease?
faq.a: A single base change can alter an amino‑acid, disrupting protein structure or function.

faq.q: How can a normal lab be misleading?
faq.a: Carrier states may have normal hemoglobin levels but still carry pathogenic alleles.

faq.q: What if genetic testing is unavailable?
faq.a: Use phenotype‑driven clinical criteria and family history to guide management.
